prompt.context: Your client is a mobile service provider in an Asian country. They were targeting the high and medium segments in the country. Recently they acquired another service provider which targeted the lower segment of the market. The two companies had two different brands before, and they kept both brands after the merger.
prompt.question: To the CEO's surprise, the overall pre-tax profit has been lower than the combined pre-tax profit of the two companies when they were not merged. You are hired to figure out why this is happening and how the client can improve it.

framework: Use the profitability formula: Profit = (P - VC) * Volume - FC
Consider product mix across the two brands (H brand targeting high/medium segment; L brand targeting lower segment)
Costs have been optimized post-merger, so focus analysis on the revenue side: price, volume, and mix
Break the L brand into sub-segments: LM (middle income) and LL (low income)

questions.prompt: Walk through the profitability framework and identify where the problem lies.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates immediately apply Profit = (P-VC)*Volume - FC and note that cost has been optimized post-merger, therefore the issue must be on the revenue side. They should consider product mix given two brands exist. Weak candidates fail to focus on profitability or ignore the product mix dimension.

questions.prompt: Has pricing changed for either brand? Has revenue per customer changed?
questions.guidance: The pricing plans for both H and L brands have not changed. However, revenue received per customer per month has been flat for the H brand but has been DECREASING for the L brand. This should direct the candidate to focus on the L brand and examine either volume or mix within it.

questions.prompt: Volume is flat for the L brand. What could explain the declining revenue per customer if pricing plans have not changed?
questions.guidance: The L brand has two sub-segments: LM (middle income) and LL (low income). The mix has been shifting toward LL (the lower-priced plan). This mix shift is the driver of declining average revenue per customer in the L brand. Volume is flat overall, so volume is not the cause.

questions.prompt: Why has the customer mix in the L brand shifted toward the lower sub-segment (LL)?
questions.guidance: Candidates should brainstorm: customer demand shift, competitor actions, product cannibalization, or 4P changes. The key insight is that the company promoted heavily on the LL plan, attracting more customers to that sub-segment. Candidates should recognize that this promotion did NOT cause cannibalization within L brand or between H and L brands, so the remaining hypothesis is that the LL promotion pulled customers away from LM — or that competitors won the LM customers.

questions.prompt: How would you verify whether competitor actions caused LM customers to leave?
questions.guidance: Review the historical customer database to identify churned LM customers. Conduct customer surveys targeting churned customers asking: (1) Why did they leave? (2) Who did they choose instead and why? This triangulates whether the mix shift was driven by external competitive pressure versus internal promotional cannibalization.

brainstorming.prompt: What could explain the mix shift in the L brand toward the lower income sub-segment (LL)?

categories.name: Internal / Company Actions
ideas: Heavy promotion on the LL plan attracted incremental customers to the lower tier
Pricing or plan design made LL more attractive relative to LM
Sales force incentivized to sell LL plans

categories.name: Customer Demand Shift
ideas: Macro-economic conditions caused LM customers to trade down to LL
Changing customer preferences toward cheaper plans

categories.name: Competitor Actions
ideas: A competitor entered the LM space, winning away LM customers
Competitor improved their LM-equivalent offer, reducing client's LM base

categories.name: Product Cannibalization
ideas: LL plan features crept upward, making it a substitute for LM
LM customers self-migrated to LL to save money

recommendation: The decline in overall profit post-merger is driven by a mix shift within the L brand toward the lower-priced LL sub-segment, reducing average revenue per customer
The mix shift was triggered by heavy promotion on the LL plan; investigate whether it also reflects LM customer loss to competitors
risks: Continuing LL promotion without addressing LM retention will further erode average revenue
If competitor displacement of LM customers is not addressed, structural revenue decline will persist
next_steps: Survey churned LM customers to determine whether they left due to competitive pressure or self-downgraded to LL
Evaluate whether the LL promotion ROI is positive when accounting for revenue cannibalization from LM
Design targeted retention or upgrade offers for LM customers to defend that higher-value sub-segment
